title: Multiroute Pathogen Transmission is Different
gist: Samuel Scarpino argues in a Science Advances Focus article that the growing list of pathogens transmitted by more than one route — HIV, hepatitis C, Zika, Ebola, mpox — behaves fundamentally differently from single-route pathogens, and that epidemiological models are only beginning to catch up. A companion multiroute model of mpox in the DRC suggests the shift toward child infections may be explained by simultaneous transmission routes rather than evolutionary change in the virus.

insights.claim: The list of pathogens transmissible by more than one route is growing rapidly and includes HIV, hepatitis C, Zika, Ebola, and mpox viruses.
insights.speaker: Santa Fe Institute
insights.so_what: Outbreak forecasting built on single-route assumptions is increasingly mis-specified for the pathogens most likely to cause the next disruption.
insights.quote: From HIV and hepatitis C to Zika, Ebola, and mpox viruses, the list of pathogens that can be transmitted in more than one way is growing rapidly.
insights.locator: From HIV and hepatitis C to Zika

insights.claim: Multiroute pathogens behave far differently from single-route pathogens, so new modelling techniques are required to capture their dynamics.
insights.speaker: Santa Fe Institute
insights.so_what: Model risk in epidemic projections is structural, not parameter noise — relevant to anyone pricing pandemic scenarios off published forecasts.
insights.quote: Multiroute pathogens don't behave like single-route ones, and the models are only starting to catch up.
insights.locator: Multiroute pathogens don't behave like single-route ones

themes.theme: Mpox in the DRC: routes, not mutation

insights.claim: When mpox began affecting children more often than adults in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, some researchers attributed the shift to evolutionary change in the virus, but a multiroute transmission model suggests simultaneous transmission routes alone could account for the shifting age pattern.
insights.speaker: Santa Fe Institute
insights.so_what: Attributing epidemiological shifts to viral evolution when transmission structure explains them can misdirect vaccine and surveillance spending.
insights.quote: some researchers thought the virus had changed evolutionarily
insights.locator: When mpox started to affect children more often

insights.claim: Infectious-disease epidemiologists will in the near future need to account for multiple transmission routes as a default when studying pathogens.
insights.speaker: Santa Fe Institute
insights.so_what: Signals a methodological shift in the discipline that will reshape which outbreak forecasts public-health agencies trust.

insights.claim: Mathematical and computational tools have begun to embrace epidemics as complex systems, but real advance requires continually challenging models against real-world data and cooperating internationally and across disciplines.
insights.speaker: Santa Fe Institute
insights.so_what: Progress depends on cross-border data sharing, making epidemic preparedness hostage to the same geopolitical fragmentation affecting other scientific commons.
